summary: Specifies how to use the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) to carry user data packets with the Host Identity Protocol. It supplies the data-protection part to go with HIP's key setup. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 7402.

eli5.summary: After two computers agree on secret keys with HIP, this paper describes the locked envelope used to send the real messages.

subtitle: How to protect user data in the Host Identity Protocol using encrypted packets.

tldr.problem: The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) establishes authenticated key material between hosts but does not specify how to protect the actual user data traffic between them.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol defines how to use the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), the same encryption and authentication protocol used in IPsec, to protect user data. It specifies how keys are drawn from HIP-generated key material, how Security Associations are set up during the HIP handshake, and how to rekey when needed.
tldr.outcome: HIP hosts can now protect user data traffic end-to-end using standard ESP mechanisms, with the Host Identity (a public key) serving as the permanent identifier. RFC 5202 is experimental and was replaced by RFC 7402.

facts.label: SPI selection
facts.value: Random, different for each HIP exchange and rekey

today: RFC 5202 is an Experimental specification that has been replaced by RFC 7402, which incorporates lessons learned from implementations and deployments.

sections.title: Using ESP for User Data in HIP
sections.content: The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) is a way for two computers to identify themselves by their public keys rather than their IP addresses. During the HIP base exchange, the computers authenticate each other and create shared key material using a Diffie-Hellman key exchange, but the RFC does not specify how to protect the actual user data they then send. This RFC fills that gap by defining how to use the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), the encryption and authentication protocol from IPsec, to protect user data packets after the HIP handshake. ESP is the standard choice for this purpose in HIP, and this document specifies the exact rules for using it. Each HIP association is linked to two ESP Security Associations (SAs), one for traffic flowing in each direction, and keys are drawn from the HIP key material during the base exchange.
sections.eli5: HIP creates shared secrets between two computers. This RFC says: use those secrets to encrypt and sign every data packet that flows between them.

sections.title: Security Associations and Key Material
sections.content: An ESP Security Association (SA) is a set of parameters that defines how packets are encrypted and authenticated in one direction. For a HIP association, two SAs are created: SA-RI (Responder-to-Initiator) and SA-IR (Initiator-to-Responder). Each SA is identified by a Security Parameter Index (SPI), a 32-bit number chosen randomly by the receiver and communicated to the sender during the handshake. The Initiator specifies the SPI it wants to receive in the I2 (second) message of the handshake. The Responder specifies the SPI it wants to receive in the R2 (fourth) message. The keys for both SAs are drawn from the KEYMAT, the keying material generated during the HIP base exchange. After HIP keys are drawn, the ESP keys are drawn in a defined order: the initiator's outgoing encryption and authentication keys, then the responder's outgoing encryption and authentication keys. The protocol mandates AES-128 for encryption and HMAC-SHA-1 for authentication. All implementations must also support NULL encryption paired with HMAC for cases where authentication is desired without encryption.
sections.eli5: Each direction of traffic has a separate set of encryption and authentication keys. The number (SPI) identifies which keys to use. Keys come from the secret that HIP created.

sections.title: Setting Up ESP Security Associations
sections.content: ESP SA setup happens during the HIP base exchange, which consists of four messages: I1 (Initiator packet 1), R1 (Responder packet 1), I2, and R2. The R1 message carries an ESP_TRANSFORM parameter listing the encryption and authentication algorithms the Responder supports. The Initiator receives this list, selects one transform, includes it in the I2 message, and specifies the SPI it wants to use for incoming traffic (in the ESP_INFO parameter). The Responder receives the I2, creates both incoming and outgoing ESP SAs, and in the R2 message sends its own SPI (the SPI value the Initiator must use for packets sent to the Responder). Once R2 is processed, both hosts have complete ESP SAs and can immediately begin exchanging encrypted user data. The protocol ensures that before user data is sent, both sides have the same cryptographic material and parameter settings, verified by HMAC and signatures embedded in the handshake messages.
sections.eli5: During the four-message handshake, the hosts negotiate encryption algorithms, exchange the SPI numbers, and derive the keys. At the end, both hosts have identical encryption rules.

sections.title: Protecting User Data Packets
sections.content: Once the ESP SAs are established, outgoing user data packets are encrypted and authenticated using the corresponding SA. For each packet, the encryption algorithm (e.g., AES-CBC) encrypts the packet payload, and the authentication algorithm (e.g., HMAC-SHA-1) computes a message authentication code over the entire encrypted packet and header. A 64-bit sequence number in the ESP header is mandatory for replay protection; packets with replayed sequence numbers are discarded. The destination IP address and the SPI in the ESP header uniquely identify the receiving HIP association, allowing the receiver to locate the correct SA for decryption and authentication. The receiver decrypts the packet, verifies the authentication code, checks the sequence number for replay, and delivers the decrypted payload to the application. The protocol supports both transport mode (where the packet source and destination are unchanged) and BEET mode (where the IP header can be rewritten while the integrity of the inner packet is preserved).
sections.eli5: Each packet is encrypted with a key only the other host knows, then signed so the receiver can confirm it came from the right place and was not tampered with.

sections.title: Updating ESP Keys
sections.content: Over the lifetime of a HIP association, the ESP SAs may need to be updated. The most common reason is sequence number exhaustion; the protocol mandates 64-bit sequence numbers, and when the counter approaches 2^64, a new SA with a new sequence number must be created. Rekeying is initiated using HIP UPDATE messages, which allow the hosts to exchange new SPI values and new key material without terminating the association. The initiating host sends an UPDATE message with the old and new SPI values and optionally a new Diffie-Hellman key (if new keying material must be generated). The responding host acknowledges with its own UPDATE containing its old and new SPI values. Both hosts then derive new keys from the KEYMAT at the specified index. During the transition, both hosts maintain both old and new SAs until traffic appears on the new association, at which point the old SA can be safely deleted. The protocol ensures that no packets are lost during rekeying because the SAs overlap momentarily.
sections.eli5: When keys get old or sequence numbers run out, the hosts exchange new keys without dropping the connection. Old packets still work while new packets arrive on the new keys.

sections.title: Implementation and Coexistence with IPsec
sections.content: The HIP implementation must coexist with standard IPsec implementations on the same host. To avoid SPI collisions, the HIP implementation MUST ensure that SPI values used for HIP SAs are not used for standard IPsec SAs, and vice versa. The Security Policy Database (SPD) must correctly route packets to the appropriate SA (HIP or IPsec). The implementation must handle the fact that HIP uses Host Identity Tags (HITs) as source and destination addresses within the protocol, but IP addresses in the actual packet headers sent over the network. Two approaches are supported: one uses a standards-compliant IPsec implementation with address translation; the other uses BEET mode, which treats the packet as transport mode internally but can rewrite the IP header. The HIP implementation SHOULD generate random SPIs following the rules in RFC 4303, and MUST generate a new SPI for each new HIP exchange and again whenever rekeying occurs.
sections.eli5: HIP can run on the same computer as standard encryption. They must not interfere with each other; HIP manages its own encryption separately from any IPsec policies.
